posts.title: Leila: from the picking aisle to the C+E cab
posts.excerpt: How former warehouse picker Leila Haddad progressed through our seven-week training framework in Ashby Vale to qualify as an articulated lorry driver.
posts.content:
For nearly four years, Leila Haddad watched articulated lorries reverse into the loading docks at her distribution centre in the East Midlands. Working as a forklift operator and warehouse picker, she spent eight hours a day moving pallets of consumer goods, checking manifests, and watching delivery drivers uncouple trailers before heading out on long-distance runs. Leila enjoyed logistics, but she knew she did not want to remain indoors moving freight between racking aisles. She wanted to sit in the cab, manage her own vehicle, and haul forty tonnes of payload across the country. In late 2026, she made the decision to retrain and contacted Kamotsu Academy in Ashby Vale.

Leila's first visit to Bay 4 at Hollins Freight Park was for an assessment drive on a crisp Tuesday morning. Course coordinator Priya Natarajan welcomed her into the office, checked her Category B car licence, and explained the training roadmap. Leila then spent two hours in an 18-tonne rigid lorry with lead instructor Ruth Abernethy, exploring basic commercial controls, wide turns, and cab visibility. Ruth noted her steady road awareness and calm reactions, recommending our combined C then C+E pathway. The £120 fee for the assessment was credited toward her course booking, and Priya immediately scheduled her Group 2 medical with an approved doctor.

Weeks 1 and 2 moved quickly. Leila passed her driver medical examination, submitted her D4 application for provisional commercial entitlement, and attended two evening theory coaching sessions in our classroom. Surrounded by highway code booklets and hazard perception practice screens, she gained clarity on braking distances, driver hours regulations, and tachograph rules. By week 3, Leila had passed both her theory and hazard perception examinations on her first attempt, allowing Priya to confirm her practical test date for week 7 with the testing authority.

Week 4 brought Leila into the 1.4-hectare yard for her first full training days. Every morning began at 07:30 with the mandatory walk-round inspection, checking tyres, wheel security, air line pressure, and vehicle lighting with instructor Kofi Mensah. Under the guidance of yard lead Ilse Brandt, Leila learned to manage trailer coupling, connecting the red and yellow air lines, and executing multi-point reversing manoeuvres between cones in the marked testing bay. Training strictly alongside one other candidate, Leila alternated between driving and observing, absorbing crucial positioning techniques from the passenger seat.

Week 5 shifted out onto the open road, taking the lorry across urban Ashby Vale, fast dual carriageways, and winding rural routes. Senior instructor Kofi Mensah worked closely with Leila on defensive road positioning, forward gear selection, and smooth braking. In week 6, Leila faced a rigorous mock test conducted by Daniel Moreau. Having an independent instructor assess her driving under formal test conditions highlighted minor adjustments needed in mirror timing, giving Leila the exact focus required for examination week.

When week 7 arrived, Leila arrived at the yard at dawn for a calm warm-up drive with Ruth Abernethy. Taking the familiar tractor unit and 13.6-metre curtain-side trailer through local dual carriageway loops settled her early nerves. When the practical test began, Leila carried out her vehicle safety checks cleanly, completed the bay reverse without hesitation, and delivered an assured road drive. When the examiner handed her the pass certificate, Leila walked back across the yard with a wide smile, having officially completed her journey from the warehouse picking aisle to the cab of a commercial articulated lorry.

posts.title: Marcus: a bus driver learns the reversing bay
posts.content:
Marcus Bell drove a passenger bus for fifteen years. Adding Class C meant learning a different kind of reversing: no mirrors on the left, a long box behind him and a bay marked in cones.

Daniel Moreau had him walk the bay before he drove it. Two trainees per lorry meant long stretches of cab time, and by the end of the yard week the bay was no longer the hard part.

posts.title: Sofia: ten years away, one refresher day
posts.content:
Sofia Ferreira drove lorries until 2016, then spent ten years away from the cab. A one-to-one refresher day was enough to get her back.

She started with the walk-round, checked the tread on each tyre with a gauge, and spent the afternoon on the road with her instructor. “It felt like a long time away, until I was back in the seat.”

posts.title: 2027 intake dates and open yard Saturdays
posts.content:
The 2027 intakes start on 12 January, 9 March, 11 May, 6 July, 14 September and 9 November, with twelve places each.

The yard is open to visitors on the first Saturday of each month from 09:00 to 12:00. Come and sit in a cab and meet the instructors.
